title: Patience in the Quran
hook: the Quran praises patient endurance and prayer
carry: patience is at the first stroke

segments.voice: Yesterday: a line the Quran says twice. Your line was it walks alongside. What ease did you find inside something hard? Today, a word the Quran reaches for when hardship comes. Day seven hundred twenty.

A woman is weeping at a grave. A man passing by stops and tells her to fear God and be patient. She snaps at him: leave me alone, you haven't been hit by what hit me. She doesn't know who he is. Later someone tells her: that was the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. She hurries to his door to apologize, and finds no guards there, just the man. And what he says to her, in the hadith collection of al-Bukhari, is one short sentence about when patience counts. Today's word is that patience.
screen: `A WOMAN WEEPING AT A GRAVE.` → `LEAVE ME ALONE.` → `SHE HURRIES TO HIS DOOR.`

segments.voice: First, the word. In Arabic it's sabr. English often says patience, but in one verse of the second chapter, Pickthall reaches for a sturdier word: "O ye who believe! Seek help in steadfastness and prayer. Lo! Allah is with the steadfast." Steadfastness. Not waiting quietly in a line. Standing your ground while something hard goes on. Second, the pairing. Sabr doesn't come alone in that verse. It comes with prayer. Endurance and turning to God are offered together, as help, not as a test you pass on your own strength. And the verse ends with a place to stand: God is with the steadfast. Third, the honesty. Two verses later, the Quran doesn't promise an easy life. It says plainly that people will be tried with some fear and hunger, with loss of wealth and lives and crops. Then it says: give good news to the steadfast. Sabr isn't the absence of hardship. It's what someone does in the middle of one. Fourth, back to the grave. The Prophet's answer to the woman, as al-Bukhari records it, is that patience is at the first stroke. Not weeks later, once the worst has passed. At the first blow. It isn't a ban on tears; in another hadith, the Prophet weeps at a death himself. Sabr, in this reading, is the first moment's choice of how to meet what has hit you: with tears if they come, but without turning on the person beside you, or on God.
screen: `SABR: STEADFASTNESS.` · `PATIENCE AND PRAYER, TOGETHER.` · `TRIED WITH FEAR AND LOSS.` · `PATIENCE AT THE FIRST STROKE.` · then, large: `ALLAH IS WITH THE STEADFAST.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath come and go. Think back to the last small blow you took. A sharp word. Bad news. A plan that fell through. Remember the first second of it: the jolt, the heat, what you said or nearly said. Now replay that first second slowly. Let the feeling be there, fully. And then, in the replay, take one breath before anything else happens. Just one. That breath is a patient moment. Rest in it for the rest of the sit. The bell holds the time.
Sabr: Arabic, patience, steadfastness. In the Quran it comes with prayer, and God is with the steadfast. Today's word.
Your line: patience is at the first stroke. Today, when the first blow of something lands, big or small, practice one patient moment: one breath before the first reply. Day seven hundred twenty.

howItsDone: Muslims speak of sabr as a virtue to practice in hardship, in daily duties and in restraint, and pair it with prayer, as the Quran does.

fork.setup: you're the woman at the grave. you snapped at a stranger, and now you learn he was the Prophet. what do you do?
options: go to his door and explain you didn't recognize him.
fork.reveal: she goes to his door, finds no guards, and he tells her that patience is at the first stroke.

original.note: Arabic: patience, steadfastness; Pickthall renders it 'steadfastness' in Quran 2:153.

trapdoor: what you thought: patience means waiting quietly for things to get better.
what it means: sabr is steadfastness in the middle of hardship, paired with prayer, and it counts most at the first blow.
what a scholar hears: sabr in Quran 2:153–157, and the hadith of the woman at the grave in Sahih al-Bukhari, 'patience is at the first stroke.'

sources.quoted: O ye who believe! Seek help in steadfastness and prayer. Lo! Allah is with the steadfast.

notes: Editor: cut the uncited general claim that Pickthall 'often' renders sabr as steadfastness (now limited to this verse); 'the word the Quran keeps reaching for' softened to 'a word'; 2:155's 'fruits of their work' corrected to 'crops' to match the verse.
'Pickthall often reaches for a sturdier word' (steadfastness) is a general description of his rendering of sabr; confirm, or reduce to 'in this verse'.
2:155 paraphrased (fear, hunger, loss of wealth, lives and crops/fruits; 'give glad tidings to the steadfast'). 2:156 is saved for day 721.

Hadith of the woman at the grave: Sahih al-Bukhari 1283 (also 1252, 1302; Sahih Muslim 926). Paraphrased; 'patience is at the first stroke' is a paraphrase in English, not a quoted translation. Confirm numbering and that the story is told accurately (no doorkeepers; 'fear Allah and be patient').
The Prophet weeping at a death: Sahih al-Bukhari 1303 (his son Ibrahim). Confirm numbering.
The closing interpretive sentence ('without turning on the person beside you, or on God') is the script's own reading; a Keeper should check it.
Auditor (2026-10-01): cut 'gently' from the hook (the hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari 1283 does not describe his tone). Pickthall 2:153 and the paraphrase of 2:155 checked.
